qs.q: A 50-year-old man with diabetes is evaluated for peripheral arterial disease. His ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) is measured, but the vascular surgeon warns that the reading may be falsely elevated. What physiological vessel change causes a falsely high ABPI in diabetic patients?
o: Severe atherosclerosis of the femoral artery
qs.e: Vessel calcification in diabetes causes arteries to become incompressible, leading to a falsely high ABPI measurement. Autonomic neuropathy causes arteriovenous shunting and warm feet, but does not directly cause incompressible vessels during blood pressure cuff inflation.

qs.q: A 70-year-old woman with peripheral arterial disease has a clean surgical incision on her foot that fails to heal after minor podiatric surgery. Which pathophysiological factor is the primary local contributor to this impaired healing process?
qs.e: Poor blood supply and hypoxia (due to peripheral arterial disease, venous stasis, or pressure) are key local factors impairing wound healing. Neutrophils normally clear debris early on and do not cause chronic surgical site ischemia.

faq.a: In critical limb ischemia, rapidly progressive claudication limiting daily activities, or when medical therapy fails to improve walking distance.

exam: A 58‑year‑old smoker presents with calf pain after walking 100 m. Which bedside test confirms PAD and what threshold defines disease? — Ankle‑brachial index; ABI ≤ 0.90.
You find an ABI of 1.35 in a diabetic patient. How do you assess arterial disease? — Use toe‑brachial index; a value ≤ 0.70 indicates PAD.
A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy develops intermittent claudication. Which additional cause should you consider? — HIV‑associated vasculopathy or drug‑induced dyslipidaemia.
What is the first pharmacologic step after diagnosing PAD and why? — Low‑dose aspirin to reduce thrombotic events; it is inexpensive and widely available.

A patient with rest pain has a non‑healing ulcer. What red flag does this represent and what immediate action is required? — Critical limb ischemia; arrange urgent vascular assessment for possible revascularisation.
How does supervised exercise improve PAD symptoms without surgery? — Improves collateral circulation and muscle efficiency, increasing walking distance.
Why should clopidogrel be avoided in a patient with severe anemia? — Increased bleeding risk without proven superiority over aspirin in PAD.
Differentiate PAD from spinal stenosis on history and exam. — PAD pain is exertional, relieved by rest; spinal stenosis improves with flexion and may have neurogenic symptoms.
ai.title: Peripheral Arterial Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is atherosclerotic narrowing of lower‑extremity arteries causing ischemic symptoms. Diagnosis relies on history, physical exam and simple bedside tests, with staging guiding management.

b: Intermittent claudication: reproducible leg pain after walking 50–200 m, relieved by rest
Critical limb ischemia: rest pain, ulceration or gangrene
Ankle‑brachial index (ABI) ≤ 0.90 confirms PAD
sections.p: PAD is chronic atherosclerotic obstruction of arteries supplying the limbs, most often the femoropopliteal segment. It is diagnosed when symptoms or objective tests show reduced arterial flow.

t.b: Is there hemodynamically significant arterial narrowing? – ABI ≤ 0.90 indicates PAD; 0.91‑1.30 is normal; > 1.30 suggests non‑compressible arteries (often in diabetes).
Are peripheral pulses diminished? – Weak or absent dorsalis pedis/posterior tibial pulses suggest proximal disease.
Where is the lesion? – Pressure drop > 20 mmHg between adjacent segments localises the obstruction.

b: Fontaine I: asymptomatic (ABI ≤ 0.90)
Fontaine IIa: intermittent claudication, ABI 0.70‑0.90
Fontaine IIb: claudication, ABI 0.40‑0.69
Fontaine III: rest pain, ABI 0.40‑0.20
Fontaine IV: ulceration/gangrene, ABI < 0.20
sections.p: The Fontaine and Rutherford classifications translate symptoms and ABI into stages that predict prognosis and guide therapy.

b: Atherosclerotic risk factors: smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidaemia
HIV‑associated vasculopathy
Tuberculosis‑related arterial inflammation
Sickle‑cell disease vaso‑occlusion
Herbal or traditional remedies causing vasospasm
sections.p: Atherosclerosis is the dominant cause, but in low‑resource East African settings additional contributors are common.

b: Intermittent claudication – cramping pain after walking a predictable distance
Rest pain – usually at night, relieved by dangling the foot over the bed
Non‑healing ulcer or gangrene on toes or foot
Cold, shiny skin, hair loss on the affected limb
sections.p: Patients usually report leg discomfort on exertion, but presentation varies with severity and comorbidities.

b: Bedside ABI – cheap, reproducible, requires only a sphygmomanometer and Doppler
Duplex ultrasound – confirms stenosis, maps disease extent if a machine exists
Plain X‑ray of foot – looks for calcified arteries, osteomyelitis in ulcers
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, bedside tools are prioritized; imaging is added when available.

t.b: What is the anatomic location and severity? – Shows peak systolic velocity ratio > 2.5 for ≥ 50 % stenosis; can guide revascularisation.
Is endovascular therapy feasible? – Visualises lesion length and calcification; not essential for initial management.

b: Rest pain lasting > 2 weeks
Non‑healing ulcer > 1 month
Rapidly progressing gangrene
Acute arterial embolism – sudden severe pain, pallor, pulselessness
sections.p: Prompt recognition of limb‑threatening disease prevents amputation and death.

b: Risk‑factor modification: stop smoking, control BP, glucose, lipids; diet low in saturated fat
Supervised exercise programme – walking 30‑45 min, 3‑5 days/week improves walking distance
Statin therapy – high‑intensity rosuvastatin or atorvastatin for all PAD patients
Wound care and off‑loading for ulcers
Revascularisation (angioplasty or bypass) for Fontaine III‑IV or lifestyle‑limiting claudication when feasible
sections.p: Treat underlying atherosclerosis, relieve symptoms, and protect the limb.

b: ABI measurement every 6‑12 months
Check smoking status, BP, HbA1c, lipid panel each visit
Inspect feet weekly; educate on footwear and hygiene
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce systemic inflammation
sections.p: Regular review monitors disease progression and treatment adherence.

b: Peripheral neuropathy (diabetic) – pain is burning, not exertional, and pulses are normal
Chronic venous insufficiency – edema, varicose veins, stasis ulcer, ankle swelling
Musculoskeletal claudication (spinal stenosis) – pain improves with flexion, not walking distance
sections.p: Conditions that cause leg pain or ulceration may mimic PAD.

b: Non‑compressible arteries in diabetes or chronic kidney disease give ABI > 1.30; toe‑brachial index is more reliable
Cold environment reduces ABI accuracy; warm the limb before measurement
Severe anemia can mask claudication pain, leading to under‑recognition
sections.p: Certain circumstances give false‑negative or false‑positive findings.

whenToSeekHelp: Rest pain or ulcer that worsens despite basic care
Signs of acute limb ischemia (pain, pallor, poikilothermia, pulselessness, paralysis)
